title: Yugoslav Workers' Self-Management Introduced in Bosnia
description: Yugoslavia introduced the self-management system, giving workers' councils formal authority over factories and enterprises across Bosnia and Herzegovina. This marked a decisive departure from Soviet-style central planning and became the defining feature of Yugoslav socialism for decades. Bosnian workers gained nominal control over production decisions in major industrial plants including the Zenica steelworks and Tuzla coal mines.

title: Yugoslav Constitutional Reform Expands Bosnia's Powers
description: The 1953 'Brioni Constitution' expanded the powers of constituent republics including Bosnia and Herzegovina, granting greater control over local economic and administrative matters. The reform moved Yugoslavia toward a more federated structure and gave Bosnia's government greater autonomy in directing development funds. It also left unresolved the political status of Bosnian Muslims, who were pressured to declare as Serbs or Croats in the 1953 census.

title: Mostar Aluminum Plant Construction Begins
description: Construction began on a major aluminum smelter near Mostar in Herzegovina, utilizing regional bauxite deposits and hydroelectric power from Neretva River dams. The plant was designed to produce aluminum for Yugoslav industry and export, diversifying Bosnia's industrial base beyond coal and steel. Mostar's economic profile shifted substantially with this flagship federal investment.

title: SFRY Constitution Enshrines Bosnia as Equal Federal Republic
description: Yugoslavia adopted a new constitution in 1963, officially proclaiming the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and further enshrining the self-management system. Bosnia and Herzegovina was formally constituted as one of six equal socialist republics within the federation, with guaranteed autonomy over natural resources, taxation, and development planning. The constitution provided a legal framework for Bosnia's distinct republican identity within a multinational socialist state.

title: Removal of Ranković Opens Space for Bosnian Muslims
description: The removal of Serbian communist hardliner Aleksandar Ranković from power at the Brioni Plenum was a watershed political moment that directly benefited Bosnia's Muslims. Ranković's secret police had disproportionately targeted Muslims, and his fall opened space for greater recognition of Muslim national identity. The event accelerated political rehabilitation of Bosnian Muslims within the Yugoslav system and emboldened Muslim intellectuals and party members to press for formal national recognition.

title: Bosnian Muslims Formally Recognized as a Distinct Nation
description: The League of Communists of Bosnia and Herzegovina formally recognized Bosnian Muslims as a distinct nation at its plenary session, a decision endorsed at the federal level and reflected in subsequent census categories. For the first time, Bosnian Muslims could identify as 'Muslim' in a national rather than merely religious sense on official documents. This historic decision was a cornerstone of Bosnian identity politics and laid the groundwork for later Bosniak national consciousness.

title: Sarajevo Selected to Host 1984 Winter Olympics
description: Sarajevo was selected as the host city for the 1984 Winter Olympics, a major international recognition of Bosnia's capital and of Yugoslavia's standing in the world. The announcement triggered major investment in sports infrastructure, roads, hotels, and urban development that transformed Sarajevo. The Olympic bid's success demonstrated Bosnia's capacity to operate on the world stage and mobilized republican and federal resources for a decade of construction.

title: Yugoslav Constitution of 1974 Grants Bosnia Near-Sovereign Powers
description: Yugoslavia's 1974 constitution, the most decentralized in the federation's history, granted republics including Bosnia near-sovereign powers and significantly reduced federal authority. Bosnia gained extensive autonomy over its legal, economic, cultural, and resource affairs, including formal authority over coal, minerals, and hydroelectric power. The constitution also introduced a collective state presidency to manage post-Tito succession, ensuring all republics including Bosnia shared executive power.

title: Alija Izetbegović Tried and Imprisoned for Islamic Declaration
description: Alija Izetbegović, a Bosnian Muslim lawyer and intellectual, was tried by Yugoslav authorities for his 'Islamic Declaration,' a text that called for Islamic social organization and was deemed subversive of the socialist order. He received a prison sentence — later reduced — that made him a prominent dissident figure and eventually a national hero among Bosnian Muslims. The trial became a landmark in Bosnian Muslim political consciousness and foreshadowed his emergence as Bosnia's wartime president.

title: Tito Dies — Bosnia Enters Collective Presidency Era
description: President Josip Broz Tito died on May 4, 1980, leaving Yugoslavia without its unifying leader after 35 years in power. The rotating collective federal presidency he designed took effect, with Bosnia's representative assuming a turn at the head of state. His death marked the beginning of a decade of political and economic instability — deepening debt, hyperinflation, and rising nationalism — that would eventually lead to Yugoslavia's dissolution.

title: Izetbegović and Muslim Intellectuals Tried for Pan-Islamic Activity
description: Alija Izetbegović and twelve Bosnian Muslim intellectuals were put on trial in Sarajevo in the 'Sarajevo Process,' charged with hostile activity inspired by Muslim nationalism and conspiring to create an Islamic state. Izetbegović received a 14-year sentence, later reduced; all defendants were released by 1988. The trial became a rallying point for Bosnian Muslim national consciousness and cemented Izetbegović's standing as a political martyr.

title: Sarajevo Hosts XIV Winter Olympic Games
description: Sarajevo hosted the XIV Winter Olympic Games from February 8–19, 1984, welcoming 1,272 athletes from 49 countries in a globally televised spectacle that attracted 2.5 billion viewers. The Games were widely regarded as a great success, showcasing Sarajevo's modernity and Bosnia's multi-cultural character to the world. Olympic infrastructure — including the Zetra ice hall, the Trebević bobsled track, and the Olympic Village — was converted to civilian use, permanently transforming the city.

title: Serbian Academy Memorandum Alarms Bosnian Leadership
description: The Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts circulated a controversial memorandum claiming Serbs were discriminated against in Yugoslavia and calling for revision of the 1974 constitutional framework. The document was seen in Bosnia as an existential threat to Bosnian sovereignty and Muslim rights, providing ideological justification for the Serbian nationalism that would drive the 1990s wars. Bosnian politicians recognized the danger but were unable to mount an effective response to the nationalist tide.

title: Agrokomerc Financial Scandal Devastates Bosnian Muslim Leadership
description: The Agrokomerc scandal exploded in August 1987 when the northwest Bosnian food conglomerate was found to have issued approximately $750 million in unsecured promissory notes, triggering a financial crisis. The scandal implicated Hamdija Pozderac, a leading Bosnian Muslim politician and member of the federal presidency, who was forced to resign in September 1987. The affair severely damaged the credibility of Bosnia's communist leadership and Bosnian Muslim political representation at the most critical moment in Yugoslav history.

title: Bosnia Holds First Multi-Party Elections — Ethnic Parties Dominate
description: Bosnia and Herzegovina held its first multi-party elections in November 1990, resulting in ethnic nationalist parties winning the vast majority of seats: Izetbegović's SDA won the Muslim vote, Karadžić's SDS won the Serb vote, and the HDZ won the Croat vote. The three parties formed a fragile coalition government that immediately faced the crisis of Yugoslavia's disintegration. The election reflected the ethno-national polarization of Bosnian society and set the stage for the coming conflict.

title: Bosnian Serbs Proclaim Autonomous Regions, JNA Arms Serbian Forces
description: Bosnian Serb leaders proclaimed Serbian Autonomous Regions across parts of Bosnia with significant Serb populations, directly challenging Bosnian territorial integrity. Simultaneously, the Yugoslav People's Army covertly transferred heavy weapons and equipment to Serbian militias, giving Bosnian Serb forces a massive military advantage before conflict erupted. The parallel political and military preparations created the conditions for the war that would follow within months.

title: Bosnian Independence Referendum and Declaration of Sovereignty
description: A referendum on Bosnian independence was held on February 29–March 1, 1992, with approximately 99.7% of voters supporting independence on a 63.4% turnout, as Bosnian Serbs largely boycotted. Bosnia declared independence on March 3, 1992, receiving international recognition from the EC and US in April. The declaration — opposed by Bosnian Serb leaders backed by Serbia — directly triggered the outbreak of war.

title: Bosnian War Begins — Siege of Sarajevo and Ethnic Cleansing
description: The Bosnian War began in April 1992 when Bosnian Serb forces backed by the JNA launched military operations across the country, beginning the 44-month siege of Sarajevo — the longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare. A systematic campaign of ethnic cleansing in eastern Bosnia targeted Muslim populations in Foča, Višegrad, and Zvornik through mass killings, rape, and forced deportation. These actions were later characterized as crimes against humanity and genocide by international tribunals.

title: UN Arms Embargo Imposed — Bosnian Government Disadvantaged
description: The UN Security Council imposed an arms embargo on all of former Yugoslavia under Resolution 713, which severely disadvantaged the poorly-armed Bosnian government forces compared to Bosnian Serb forces that had inherited the JNA's arsenal. Bosnia's government and many Western observers criticized the embargo as effectively aiding the aggressor. Debates over lifting or circumventing the embargo became a central international controversy throughout the war.

title: Croat-Muslim War Erupts — Stari Most Bridge Destroyed
description: A war broke out between Bosnian Croat HVO forces and Bosnian government forces in 1993, transforming the conflict into a three-sided war and including the Ahmići massacre by HVO forces. On November 9, 1993, HVO artillery deliberately destroyed the 16th-century Stari Most bridge in Mostar — a UNESCO-recognized cultural landmark and symbol of Ottoman heritage. The destruction was widely condemned as an act of cultural terrorism and severely weakened Bosnia's military capacity to resist Bosnian Serb forces.

title: Washington Agreement Ends Croat-Muslim War
description: The Washington Agreement of March 1994 ended the Bosnian Croat-Muslim conflict and created the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, joining Bosniak and Croat forces under a unified military command. Brokered by the United States, the agreement significantly improved the military position of non-Serbian forces and provided a constitutional foundation for one of the two post-war entities. It was a critical diplomatic turning point enabling the eventual Dayton framework.

title: Markale Marketplace Massacre Triggers NATO Ultimatum
description: A mortar shell struck the Markale marketplace in Sarajevo in February 1994, killing 68 civilians and wounding over 140 in the single deadliest incident of the Sarajevo siege to that point. The massacre shocked the world and triggered NATO's first ultimatum to Bosnian Serb forces to withdraw heavy weapons from around Sarajevo within 10 days or face air strikes. The episode marked a turning point in international resolve to impose consequences on Bosnian Serb forces.

title: Srebrenica Genocide — 8,000 Bosniak Men and Boys Executed
description: In July 1995, following the fall of the UN 'safe area' of Srebrenica to Bosnian Serb forces commanded by General Ratko Mladić, approximately 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were systematically executed in the largest mass killing in Europe since World War II. The International Court of Justice and the ICTY subsequently ruled the killings constituted genocide, committed with the specific intent to destroy Bosnian Muslims as a group. The Srebrenica massacre remains the defining atrocity of the Bosnian War and a central trauma in Bosnian and international memory.

title: NATO Operation Deliberate Force Breaks Bosnian Serb Military Power
description: Following the second Markale massacre and the Srebrenica genocide, NATO launched Operation Deliberate Force in August–September 1995, conducting intensive air strikes against Bosnian Serb military targets. The campaign degraded Bosnian Serb military capabilities and combined with a Croat-Bosniak ground offensive that dramatically shifted the military balance, recovering significant territory. The operations directly compelled Bosnian Serb forces to the negotiating table that produced the Dayton Agreement.

title: Dayton Peace Agreement Ends Bosnian War
description: The General Framework Agreement for Peace — the Dayton Agreement — was initialed at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base on November 21, 1995, and formally signed in Paris on December 14. The agreement ended the war, preserved Bosnia as a single sovereign state divided into the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, and established the Office of the High Representative to oversee civilian implementation. The Dayton Agreement has governed Bosnia's constitutional and political structure ever since.

title: First Post-War Elections Institutionalize Ethnic Divisions
description: Bosnia held its first post-war elections in September 1996 under OSCE supervision, establishing the joint institutions mandated by the Dayton Agreement — a tripartite presidency and Parliamentary Assembly. Nationalist parties dominated across all three ethnic groups, and the elections were criticized for irregular practices and for institutionalizing ethnic divisions rather than promoting reconciliation. Simultaneously, approximately 62,000 Sarajevo Serbs departed for Republika Srpska as city suburbs were transferred to Bosnian government control.

title: Bonn Powers Granted to High Representative
description: The Peace Implementation Council meeting in Bonn in December 1997 granted the High Representative sweeping executive powers to impose laws and remove obstructive officials from office. This transformed the OHR from a monitoring body into an executive authority capable of forcing Dayton implementation against nationalist obstruction. The Bonn Powers were exercised extensively over the following decade, removing dozens of officials and imposing hundreds of laws across both entities.

title: Brcko Designated Self-Governing District Under Both Entities
description: The Brcko arbitration tribunal issued its final award in March 1999, designating Brcko as a self-governing district simultaneously under the jurisdiction of both entities — neither controlled exclusively by Republika Srpska nor the Federation. The decision prevented Republika Srpska from maintaining full territorial contiguity and created a unique constitutional unit that became something of a test case for multi-ethnic post-war administration. The Brcko resolution removed a key flashpoint for renewed conflict.

title: Stari Most Reconstruction Project Launched
description: International donors and governments committed to funding the reconstruction of Mostar's Stari Most bridge, destroyed by HVO artillery in 1993. The reconstruction project used original Ottoman-era techniques and local Tenelija stone sourced from the same quarry as the original 16th-century structure. The rebuilt bridge became a powerful symbol of post-war reconciliation and cultural restoration, eventually inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2005.

title: State-Level Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina Established
description: The state-level Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established with OHR support, providing Bosnia for the first time with a court capable of trying war crimes and serious organized crime at the state level. The court absorbed cases from the ICTY as the tribunal wound down its docket and handled sensitive domestic war crimes prosecutions. It was a significant step in building rule of law institutions capable of domestic accountability for wartime atrocities.

title: Paddy Ashdown Becomes High Representative, Pursues Aggressive Reform
description: British politician Lord Paddy Ashdown was appointed High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina in May 2002 and pursued an ambitious agenda of institutional reform and state-building using the Bonn Powers. His tenure saw the most assertive use of international authority in Bosnia's post-war history, including removing dozens of officials and imposing legislation on police, defense, and economic reform. Critics questioned the democratic legitimacy of governing by executive imposition, while supporters argued it was necessary to break nationalist obstruction.

title: Bosnia Launches EU Stabilization and Association Process
description: Bosnia and Herzegovina formally initiated its Stabilization and Association Agreement process with the European Union, launching the country's European integration trajectory. The SAA process required Bosnia to implement major administrative, judicial, and economic reforms as conditions for closer EU ties. European integration became the central organizing objective of Bosnian foreign policy for the following two decades.

title: Stari Most Reopened — UNESCO World Heritage Symbol Restored
description: The rebuilt Stari Most (Old Bridge) in Mostar was officially reopened on July 23, 2004, in a ceremony attended by dignitaries from across the world after five years of reconstruction using traditional Ottoman methods. The reconstruction was hailed as a powerful symbol of reconciliation and Bosnia's cultural recovery from the war, and the bridge was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2005. The reopening drew international media attention and marked a milestone in Mostar's post-war recovery.

title: EUFOR Operation Althea Replaces NATO SFOR in Bosnia
description: NATO's Stabilization Force (SFOR) was replaced by the European Union's EUFOR Operation Althea in December 2004, marking a transition of peacekeeping responsibility from NATO to the EU in Bosnia. EUFOR maintained a significant military presence to deter renewed conflict and support the civilian implementation of Dayton. The transition reflected the EU's deepening engagement with Bosnian stability as part of its broader enlargement strategy.

title: Defense Law Creates Unified Armed Forces of Bosnia
description: A Defense Law was passed in Bosnia creating a single unified Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina under state-level command, replacing the separate entity armies — the Army of the Federation and the Army of Republika Srpska. The law was a prerequisite for Bosnia's NATO integration and was achieved over significant political resistance from Bosnian Serb politicians. The unified military was widely seen as a concrete demonstration that a functional Bosnian state was possible.

title: Bosnia Joins NATO Partnership for Peace
description: Bosnia and Herzegovina formally joined NATO's Partnership for Peace program in December 2006, a milestone in its Euro-Atlantic integration journey that required completing defense reforms including army unification. The PfP membership gave Bosnia's security integration a formal framework and committed it to annual political, economic, and defense reform programs. NATO and EU accession became the twin pillars of Bosnia's external relations strategy.

title: ICJ Rules Serbia Failed to Prevent Srebrenica Genocide
description: The International Court of Justice issued a landmark ruling in February 2007 finding that genocide had occurred at Srebrenica, constituting the first time the ICJ applied the Genocide Convention to a specific conflict. While the ICJ did not find Serbia directly responsible for perpetrating the genocide, it ruled Serbia had breached the Genocide Convention by failing to prevent it and by not cooperating with the ICTY. The ruling was a watershed in international legal accountability for Bosnia's wartime experience.

title: Radovan Karadžić Arrested After 13 Years in Hiding
description: Radovan Karadžić, indicted for genocide and crimes against humanity by the ICTY, was arrested in Belgrade in July 2008 after living under an assumed identity as a New Age healer named Dragan Dabić. He was transferred to The Hague to face trial and was ultimately convicted of genocide in 2016 and sentenced to life imprisonment on appeal in 2019. His arrest was a major breakthrough in post-war justice and removed a key symbolic obstacle to Serbia's EU aspirations.

title: Sejdić-Finci Ruling — European Court Finds Bosnia Constitution Discriminatory
description: The European Court of Human Rights ruled in December 2009 in the Sejdić and Finci case that Bosnia's constitution discriminated against citizens who identify as Jewish or Roma by excluding them from running for the state presidency and House of Peoples — offices reserved for Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. Bosnia's failure to implement the ruling became a persistent obstacle to EU integration progress. The case highlighted the structurally discriminatory nature of the Dayton constitutional framework.

title: Post-Election Government Formation Crisis — 15 Months Without Government
description: The October 2010 general elections produced a fragmented result that led to over 15 months of government formation negotiations — a post-war record. Bosnia spent the period without a functioning state-level Council of Ministers, demonstrating the deep dysfunction of its ethnic power-sharing architecture. The paralysis had negative consequences for EU integration progress and investor confidence and became a symbol of Bosnia's institutional failure.

title: Ratko Mladić Arrested in Serbia After 16 Years as Fugitive
description: General Ratko Mladić, indicted for the Srebrenica genocide and the siege of Sarajevo, was arrested in Serbia in May 2011 after 16 years as a fugitive from ICTY justice. He was transferred to The Hague and ultimately convicted of genocide and war crimes in 2017, receiving a life sentence. His arrest was a momentous event for Srebrenica's survivors and a key milestone in the ICTY's accountability mission for Bosnia.

title: Bosnian Spring — Mass Protests Sweep Federation Cities
description: Mass protests erupted on February 4–5, 2014, beginning in Tuzla where laid-off workers from privatized factories including Dita, Polihem, and Guming demanded back pay and accountability after new owners stripped assets and filed for bankruptcy. The protests spread to Sarajevo, Zenica, and other Federation cities, with demonstrators attacking government buildings in the most violent unrest since the war's end. The uprising was followed by citizens' plenary assemblies (plenums) in around 20 towns — a novel direct democracy experiment reflecting cross-ethnic civic anger at corruption and unemployment.

title: Catastrophic Floods — Worst in 120 Years
description: In May 2014 Bosnia and Herzegovina was struck by the worst floods in 120 years, causing catastrophic damage along the Sava, Bosna, and Drina rivers and killing at least 60 people, with over a million affected across the region. The floods caused billions of euros in damage to infrastructure and agriculture and triggered landslides that reopened minefields from the 1992–95 war. The disaster tested Bosnia's fragmented governance structures and required international humanitarian assistance.

title: Russia Vetoes UN Srebrenica Genocide Resolution
description: A UN Security Council draft resolution declaring the Srebrenica massacre a genocide was vetoed by Russia in July 2015, to the outrage of Bosnian victims and their families. The veto, supported by China, was widely seen as political protection for Serbia and Republika Srpska, which fiercely resisted the genocide designation. The episode demonstrated how Bosnia's post-war justice remained entangled in great-power geopolitics.

title: Karadžić Convicted of Genocide, Sentenced to 40 Years (Later Life)
description: Radovan Karadžić was convicted by the ICTY on March 24, 2016, of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre, persecution, extermination, and other crimes, receiving a 40-year sentence. The UN appeals court increased the sentence to life imprisonment in March 2019, finding the original sentence inadequately reflected the extraordinary gravity of the crimes. The conviction was a landmark in international criminal justice and confirmed genocide findings that Republika Srpska continued to deny.

title: RS Holds Illegal Referendum Defying Constitutional Court
description: Republika Srpska held a referendum in September 2016 on retaining January 9 as the official RS Day holiday, despite a ruling by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia that the date discriminated against Bosniak citizens. The referendum was declared unconstitutional and led to criminal charges against Dodik personally from the state prosecutor. The episode illustrated Dodik's systematic willingness to challenge Dayton institutions and set the stage for further secessionist escalation.

title: Bosnia Submits Formal EU Membership Application
description: Bosnia and Herzegovina formally submitted its EU membership application to the Council of the EU in February 2016, receiving an acknowledgment and a questionnaire of over 3,000 questions from the European Commission. The EU made clear that substantial reforms in rule of law, anti-corruption, and fundamental rights were needed before candidate status would be considered. Bosnia lagged behind Serbia and Montenegro in the Western Balkans EU integration queue.

title: Ratko Mladić Convicted of Genocide and Sentenced to Life
description: General Ratko Mladić was convicted by the ICTY in November 2017 of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity and sentenced to life imprisonment for his role in the Srebrenica genocide, the siege of Sarajevo, and ethnic cleansing across Bosnia. The verdict was one of the most significant in the history of international criminal law. Srebrenica survivors called the conviction justice overdue, while Republika Srpska authorities continued to reject the genocide characterization.

title: NATO Activates Membership Action Plan for Bosnia
description: NATO foreign ministers formally activated Bosnia and Herzegovina's Membership Action Plan on December 5, 2018, inviting Bosnia to submit its first annual national program of political, economic, and defense reforms. The activation was conditioned on ongoing property registration requirements and was complicated by Republika Srpska's opposition to full NATO integration. The MAP set out the formal pathway to eventual full NATO membership.

title: Dodik Launches Campaign to Dissolve State-Level Institutions
description: Milorad Dodik launched an escalating campaign in 2021 to withdraw Republika Srpska from state-level institutions — including the armed forces, judiciary, and indirect tax authority — threatening Bosnia's functional integrity and the Dayton framework. The United States imposed targeted sanctions on Dodik and associated entities in response. International observers described the crisis as the most serious threat to post-war Bosnian stability since the war's end.

title: Bosnia Granted EU Candidate Status
description: The European Commission recommended granting Bosnia and Herzegovina EU candidate status in October 2022, and the European Council formally granted it on December 15, 2022 — Bosnia's most significant EU integration milestone. The candidacy came with extensive reform conditions across rule of law, anti-corruption, and fundamental rights. The decision placed Bosnia within the formal EU accession queue alongside Serbia, Montenegro, Albania, and North Macedonia.

title: General Elections — Bećirović Defeats Dodik for Bosniak Presidency Seat
description: Bosnia held general elections in October 2022 against a backdrop of institutional crisis driven by Dodik's secessionist activities and disputes over the electoral law. Denis Bećirović narrowly defeated Dodik for the Bosniak seat on the state presidency, a significant political setback for Dodik at the state level. The High Representative used Bonn Powers on election night to impose constitutional changes related to the Croat representation dispute, prompting condemnation from Republika Srpska and Russia.

title: EU Opens Formal Accession Negotiations with Bosnia
description: The European Council unanimously approved the opening of EU accession negotiations with Bosnia and Herzegovina in March 2024, following the European Commission's recommendation that Bosnia had made sufficient reform progress. The formal opening of negotiations in June 2024 was a historic milestone in the country's European integration journey after years of delays. Substantial conditions remained — including a negotiating framework, reform package approval, and appointment of a chief negotiator — before talks could formally begin.

title: UN General Assembly Adopts Srebrenica Genocide Commemoration Resolution
description: The United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 78/282 on May 23, 2024, by 84 votes in favour to 19 against, designating July 11 as the International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica. The resolution condemned without reservation any denial of the Srebrenica genocide and the glorification of those convicted of related war crimes. The vote was hailed by genocide survivors and Bosniak leaders as an important step toward international recognition, despite opposition from Serbia, Russia, China, and Republika Srpska.

title: Dodik Sentenced to One Year in Prison for Defying High Representative
description: The Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina convicted Milorad Dodik in February 2025 and sentenced him to one year in prison and a six-year ban from public office for knowingly defying decisions issued by High Representative Christian Schmidt. An appeals court confirmed the sentence in August 2025, and Bosnia's Constitutional Court rejected his final domestic appeal in November 2025. Dodik rejected the court's jurisdiction and Republika Srpska authorities refused to enforce the ruling, creating a direct confrontation between the Dayton constitutional order and secessionist resistance.

title: Sarajevo Declares State of Emergency Over Extreme Air Pollution
description: The Sarajevo Canton government declared a state of emergency on 20 December 2023 after PM2.5 particulate pollution reached 245 micrograms per cubic meter, 49 times the WHO-tolerated level. The emergency measures banned older Euro 3 vehicles from city traffic and closed dust-emitting facilities. The pollution stemmed largely from tens of thousands of households burning wood and coal for heat combined with coal-fired power plants supplying most of the country's electricity.
